utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Before we begin to hear the evidence of the next witness, I have something to deal with before. It has been brought to the Chamber's attention that over the last couple of weeks the number of last-minute extensions to already extended sittings has increased. The Chamber recognises that this is a strain on all participants in these proceedings, and, in particular, on the interpreters. The Chamber wishes to express its gratitude for the quality of their work and their dedication. The Chamber would also ask the parties to keep to their time estimate or to the time granted by the Chamber. Finally, it would ask the Prosecution to organise the witness scheduling so that such scheduling constraints calling for last-minute extension should not occur, save on an exceptional basis, and to inform the Chamber as soon as possible when it becomes aware of such a situation. That said, if the witness could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please be seated. Good morning, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then could we begin by calling up 65 ter 90322, the pseudonym sheet for this witness. And, of course, not broadcast it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you see your name on the screen in front of you correctly spelled?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could that be the first Prosecution exhibit for this witness, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4626, under seal, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, you've given a statement to this Tribunal in the past, and you've also testified in four previous proceedings; most recently in the Tolimir case in 2010. Now, in coming to testify here today, did you have a chance to listen to a recording of your evidence in that case?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, I listened to my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You might have to lean a little bit further into the microphone when you give your answers, Witness. Were you satisfied with the accuracy of that recording?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, I am satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions today during these proceedings as you were asked in that case, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And so, Your Honours, the transcript of this witness's evidence in the Tolimir case is 65 ter 23650, and if that could be, please, the next Prosecution exhibit. I'd just like to note that 23650A is a public redacted version of that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So probably we will give two separate exhibit numbers. Yes, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 23650 should be assigned Exhibit P4627, under seal. And 65 ter 23650A should be assigned Exhibit P4628. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, to summarise that written evidence, during 1994 and 1995, this witness was involved in the monitoring, recording, and transcribing of intercepted radio signal communications involving Serbian forces and Serbian civilian leaders as well. He describes the location at which this was conducted, the staff involved, the equipment used, and all stages of the process and procedures involved in the intercepting and transcribing of these communications. He was personally involved in all aspects of this process. He explains how recordings were made of intercepted communications and how speakers were identified. Additionally, this witness has reviewed, identified and authenticated transcripts of intercepted communications prepared within the unit in which he served, including conversations he personally recorded and transcribed. And that's the brief summary of the written evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, further to that, I have some -- small number of additional questions I'd like to ask you, and I'd just like to, before we begin, caution you that if in your answers you feel you might reveal your identity, please ask for private session. Now, Mr. Witness, in your written evidence at pages 2067 to 2069, you were asked whether you shared any of your intercepts with the army and vice versa, and you explained how you made an arrangement with representatives of the PEB of the 2nd Corps to do that. So, practically speaking, can you just tell us briefly how this sharing was done?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I can't recall when exactly, but at some point, this idea came about as a necessity of sorts. There was a need to keep the military and civilian leadership of my service informed, and they believed that it would be useful if we, at the location, did not decide on what was important or not but that we should, rather, hand everything over to the 2nd Corps and then, in turn, they would provide their conversations to us. That is how we began this exchange process, although I no longer recall when exactly. We exchanged such reproduced conversations in the following way. First, they would be processed, that is to say, put in it the computer and encrypted. During the open phase, they were saved on floppy disks and exchanged as such, both ways. When they provided us with such floppy disk conversations, we only introduced a small number of measures or procedures that had previously been arranged in order to be able to identify the conversations provided by the 2nd Corps and the PEB, and we would also assign numbers to such conversations under which they were then forwarded to the seat of our service.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So other than these small number of measures you've spoken about, to identify the conversations as being provided by the 2nd Corps, did you -- did you modify them in any way at all?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: The text itself was not changed at all. There was no need. In the heading, though, such conversations received an addition. In other words, we put in a remark that this conversation came from the 2nd Corps. We also included the date and number under which we logged it and forwarded it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look quickly at P4483, please. A transcript of a conversation which took place on 16 July 1995 at 1529 between someone from the Main Staff and Palma, and it bears the ordinal number 668. Could you enlarge the B/C/S page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, we don't see this heading at the top of the English translation but perhaps you could tell us what the heading at the top of this -- the B/C/S original reads, please.

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. It contains the remark I mentioned, indicating that the conversation came from the 2nd Corps PEB for our needs. We also see in the left-hand corner the number that was used to log it and the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So from your answer I take it this is an example of the intercepts we've just been discussing?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it emanated, then, from your unit?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes. We forwarded it to our seat, the seat of our service.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this conversation has previously been marked for identification and subject to authentication discussed by a previous witness at pages 25312 to 25317 of the transcript of this trial. I'd like to ask this be admitted for all purposes now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We don't have any objection to that. We've been in communication with the Prosecution and it seems that they would like to move into evidence all of the documents that have been marked for identification once they're authenticated by a witness. I don't know if it is your desire to have further showing of the relevance of those, but as far as we're concerned, it is not necessary. So it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think in marking for identification, pending the authentication, Chamber examined the prima facie relevance and probative value of intercepts. I think that has been our practice. So whether we'll deal with it in a -- separately on a comprehensive manner or we deal with it one by one, it is up to the Prosecution. And then we have no problem in fully admitting this exhibit at the moment. We'll do that, Ms. Edgerton. It was admitted when -- marked for identification when Mr. Obradovic was here, if my memory is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, of course, it is Your Honours. Could we go over now to a conversation of another type, D2002, a conversation dated 16 July 1995 at 4.15, with the ordinal number 664 between the Main Staff duty officer and General Mladic. Can you just enlarge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, is this a conversation that was transcribed within your unit?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the difference between this one and the intercept we've just looked at appears to lie in the header and in the combination of letters and numbers at the bottom of the page. What do those letters and numbers at the bottom of the page, left-hand side, represent?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page is the code -- are the code-names or code designations of the two workers who worked on the document. The first one ending at 073 is the person who recorded the conversation. The other designation, or combination of letters and numbers, identifies the person who reproduced the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Same request, please, Your Honour, with respect to D2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But why was not marked for identification? According to the record, it say it is was fully admitted. I will consult the Registrar on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whatever status it may have been, we'll admit it fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go -- oh. Could we go now further to 65 ter 32446, a conversation dated 11 July 1995 with the ordinal number 535. And that conversation appears at the bottom of the B/C/S page in front of you, Mr. Witness, and it's a conversation between General Gvero and Dr. Karadzic. And, Mr. Registrar, if you could just indulge the witness, could I ask you to go to the second page of the B/C/S version so the witness can see the name indications at the bottom of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, having looked at this, could you tell us whether this transcript also emanated from within your unit?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to ask for this conversation to be admitted as a Prosecution exhibit and my submission would be that the relevance being absolutely obvious on the face of this conversation, Your Honours admit this for all purposes as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no opposition from the Defence on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4629, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, Ms. Edgerton, do we have to admit this under seal or publicly?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Although these were admitted in the Tolimir case, or similar intercepts, not this one, were admitted in the Tolimir case under seal, I think that in light of today's record thus far, we're able to admit this publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll come back to those items. But thank you for your guidance. We'll admit it publicly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could -- remaining on this document that we -- oh, actually, I think we'll have to call up essentially the same document under another 65 ter number. And that's 32447. And just for the record, we see 32247 on the -- on the B/C/S page in front of us, as it happens, but we'll need to have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's another conversation, just 20 minutes after the first one, between Dr. Karadzic and General Gvero that we just dealt with and it has the ordinal number 536, and we see General Gvero saying: "Mr. President, Serbian silver, Serbian church, Serbian flag," and further. Was this conversation, then, also something, Mr. Witness, having looked at it, that was recorded and transcribed by your unit?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Same request, please, Your Honours, with respect to this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'm just wondering about the last line of this intercept. I don't know if that is it part of the intercept or somebody's subjective viewpoint of other information they're receiving. So I don't know if Ms. Edgerton wants to inquire, but I think we would object to the last line unless there's other foundation to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you do not challenge the other interlocutor was Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't know. But we're taking the intercept at face value, so we understand that this is a sufficient foundation for its reliability. But, in any event, we think that the -- the intercept can be admitted but the last line should be struck absent further foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm happy to ask the question of this witness about the last line, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, there's a notation that appears at the bottom of this transcripted conversation that reads: "General Gvero is present today at the Supreme Command headquarters." Do you have any information on where that information might have been derived from?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I'll try to explain. On this channel or direction that we monitored, there were a number of lines that were tapped. That day, the operators, following all of the lines, concluded that only Gvero was there, which doesn't, of course, mean that there were no lower-ranking officers. It's not as if the building was empty. But that day, somebody must have commented upon that in another conversation, which may not have been important or reproduced, that only Gvero was present, or in one of the previous conversations, it was so said. In any case, this is what I'm trying to say. A remark like this would not be arbitrary because our intention was not to misinform. It does have a basis. The colleagues who worked on it that day introduced the remark based on something sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just one further question. When you talk about basis, Witness, on what basis would Dr. Karadzic have been identified as one of the interlocutors in these two conversations?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Now I see that Gvero is addressing Karadzic with "President." That is one argument that we relied on, since it was standard practice that Karadzic was addressed with "President."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I please renew my request to have this second intercept admitted, Your Honours, for all purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm advised that the last line hasn't actually been translated into English correctly. That there's the word "only" General Gvero was present to -- is present today that is omitted from the English translation. So perhaps it can be sent back for revision. But aside from that, I think our position is -- is that we don't object to the admission of the intercept but we call the Chamber's attention to the weight to be given to comments as opposed to -- and also identification of speakers based on deductions as opposed to what is in the actual text and we hope that you will give that less weight. Other than that, though, we think it is sufficiently reliable under the standards of the Appeals Chamber that it can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, Mr. Witness, could you kindly read the last line so that we can hear the interpretation again, which starts with "Danas." Could you read it please aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Today only General Gvero is present at the Supreme Command headquarters."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So apparently "only" is omitted from the translation. I think that's clear from the record, Mr. Robinson. Yes, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 32447 shall be assigned Exhibit P4630. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, finally, could we go to 65 ter 31269B, an intercept which took place on 18 July 1995, bearing the ordinal number 696, recorded on the Pale radio-relay route between a person identified as X and a person named Budimir. Now, to assist the witness, could you just pull up this conversation in his language so that he can go to the bottom of the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then back up to the top, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- was this -- is this another example of a conversation transcribed by and emanating from your unit?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, this is a conversation of ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, given Mr. Robinson's position, I'd like without further questions to tender this as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4631, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that would conclude my examination-in-chief. And with that, of course, I'd like to move in associated exhibits as identified in our notification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What about those -- the -- those intercepts that does -- do not have English translation? Example -- for example, 65 ter 3383 and 65 ter 32458.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I perhaps then would like to come back to you on these after the conclusion of the cross-examination because, in fact, there are English translations for all of them, and they obviously haven't been uploaded and available to Your Honours. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And my second question is whether to admit them under seal or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Subject to, in the case of a number of them, a small redaction which we're prepared to do of the names that appear, the code names and names that appear at the bottom of those intercepts, I don't see any reason for them to be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So could you come back in a more comprehensive way after this witness's evidence is over.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, as you noticed, your examination-in-chief, or evidence in-chief, was admitted in lieu of your oral testimony in written form, i.e., your testimony in Tolimir was admitted in its entirety. Now you'll be further cross-examined by Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to start with what was most recently discussed. The way in which you determined that I was on the other end of the line. You said that this form of address that was used, "Mr. President," that is what was decisive; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes. There were a few ways in which we identified the participants in a particular conversation. At any rate, as you know, as you've seen here, there are a great many conversations in which the participants were identified as X and Y. Also, we have in this latest one, we have a certain Branimir. I have no idea. At any rate, you were invariably addressed as President. That is one of the arguments for us to write up that it was you. President was the customary form of address that was used for you. We did not hear anyone else being addressed as President in these communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In our part of the world, how do people address the prime minister? Is it customary to say "Prime Minister" or "Premier," or "President," again, "predsednice"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Usually it's Premier, or "predsednice vlade," Prime Minister. In this case, I really never heard a conversation with a prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how does one address the president of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I never addressed him, but you know that the best. Probably as you look at each other into the eye, you call each other President, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the president of the municipality? How does one address the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: President of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The whole thing, invariably, or just President?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this was an exceptionally important piece of news. This was an important moment. In this important moment, I don't think that Mr. Gvero would have called the president of the municipality and said, "The Serbian flag, the Serbian silver," and so on and so forth. So if you look at the context of the conversation, in our view, the conclusion is that it was you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How does one address the president of a commission?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: It depends. You can also address him by his name. I've already said this is a very important conversation. This is a very important piece of information. This is a high-ranking officer who was providing information to someone that he is supposed to convey this important news to. I don't think there's any point in going through all of these things, president of the commission, whatever. This was our assessment at that point in time. We did not provide this conversation to anyone. We used this for our own internal purposes, and I think that we did well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While I was free, do you know that the president of the assembly, Krajisnik, actually, that they tried to ascribe this conversation, this intercept of yours, to him?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know what kind of relationship General Gvero and I had during those days?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You completed a secondary technical school; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: If you'd like to identify me, then I'd kindly ask that we move into private session or closed session. I don't know exactly how this should be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before doing that, Mr. Witness, page 16, line 8, you just said: "In this important moment" -- I will read it from that before that. This is what you said: "Mr. Karadzic, this was an exceptionally piece of news. This was an important moment. In this important moment, I don't think that Mr. Gvero would have called the president of the municipality and said, 'The Serbian flag, the Serbian silver ...'" Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that it was Gvero that called the president, whoever it may be? Would you like to see the intercept again? Yes, it's P4630.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. Yes, I see the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you know who called first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know. I don't know who called who in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, if you meant to ask some personal questions, we'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll drop that, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what I would like to ask the witness now. Is it correct, Witness, that he is not saying "Mr. President" in this case. He is only saying "President." And was this recorded verbatim?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I'll try to explain this to you. This phenomenon that may occur. Sometimes the name is dropped or the form of address or the first part of a sentence, because the operator who is sitting there, at the moment when the conversation starts, the interlocutor can introduce himself or say, please, or there can be a telephone operator who is linking them up, and then he is late when he starts the recording so then that part remains missing or unrecorded. So this is an authentic recording. None of the operators could change that, you see. Perhaps sometimes an operator could point out that a formal address was heard, and then if, on the basis of that, if he heard, This is Gvero speaking, please may I speak to this or that person. Then he would write down that it was Gvero who is the person in question. You see, in this conversation, Gvero did not introduce himself either, if I see this right. I think that's the way it was. He didn't introduce himself either. But we have these previous conversations. So after 20 minutes, a new conversation took place between the same interlocutors. So this is linked to the previous conversation. So you can take the previous conversation perhaps and then it will all become clear to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But, Mr. Witness, where it says "after 20 minutes" and so on and so forth, all of these are the positions of the operator or the observations of the operator instead of writing down exactly what the time was and exactly what was being said; right? This is his comment. This is his conclusion.

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I suggest to that you we look at the previous conversation as well. Perhaps there we have the exact time of the conversation recording and then, by resorting to analogy, the operator realised that 20 minutes later, this conversation took place. Let us take a look at that first and then we can comment upon this. There is nothing arbitrary about this. Nobody was trying to relativise anything. This information was very important at the time, and no one dared play any kind of games with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What do you mean useful and important? For what purposes was this done?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I cannot say. It was our task to convey this, and what this was used for afterwards and whether it was used at all, that I don't know. Believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Had this been done for a court of law, would you have done something differently?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, had this been done for a court of law, then somebody would have probably come to see us and tell us what it was that mattered to courts of law, and then all of this information would have probably had a different form. Perhaps more details and so on. I mean, each part that could be heard before the recording would start -- well, I don't know what a court would be interested in. But they would probably suggest something to us. I don't know. Maybe we would keep the written record that we would destroy after we would reproduce all of this. It would be found in headquarters, printed out. I mean, I really cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please: How did you recognise Gvero here, if he didn't introduce himself?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I've just explained that. We'd have to go back to the previous conversation, because it says here, again, we heard only Gvero, or, that is to say, a conversation between the same interlocutors. So we'd have to go back to the previous conversation. Perhaps he introduced himself there. But let me tell you, at the time we knew Gvero's voice very well. We heard him very often, and we would recognise his voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please: How much time would be missed of that initial time? How many seconds would be missed from the beginning of a conversation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Practically speaking, you can imagine yourself what the situation is like. You have this equipment on your desk and then the recording starts -- or, rather, the telephone rings and this man answers the phone immediately and says, Captain so-and-so, please go ahead, and we would press a button in order to start recording again and perhaps he would introduce himself during that split second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it's up to five seconds; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you exactly how many seconds. We'd have to measure that. But this is what it looked like in practice. You know what it's like. Somebody picks up a phone, introduces himself, and you press this button or perhaps you're a bit late because you were in another area and by the time you get there and press the button, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. Did you figure out how people talked to me on the phone during the war? Do you know that people would call and the secretary would answer the phone, and this person would say, Is the president there? And then she'd answer or she would ask me whether I was willing to speak to this person or not. Do you know that that was the procedure involved?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I believe that was the procedure, but you also know that, frequently, you and other members of the leadership were in the field and there were no secretaries. I don't know want to go into that. I can only discuss here what we heard and wrote down that. That's the whole point. Nobody made up anything. It wasn't our purpose. There was no point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This took place on the 11th of July; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the previous one? It may be of assistance to the witness. P4629.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the conversation that appears at the top of the B/C/S page, for everyone's information, is actually 65 ter 30927. That's the conversation with the ordinal number 534.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So we have to show the witness the bottom part of the page. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So at the top, we have a conversation between General Gvero and General Nicolai and Svetlana, the interpreter. Things are probably clearer there, because people introduced themselves. Now as for the conversation number 535, how did you establish who the participants were?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I've explained how. Now we go back to the time of the conversation, which is 4.23 p.m. In that conversation, we only heard Gvero. We didn't hear you, and there's a reason for that. Now go back to your story of a couple of minutes ago, when you asked me about the way the president was addressed. Now would General Gvero be informing someone at a much lower level of having discussed things with General Nicolai, and so on and so forth. That is why we were certain at the time that it concerned you. He informed you of some important things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So your conclusions, as regards the importance of that conversation, resulted in your conclusion that it was me?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: No. You were addressed as President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But there is no "Mr. President," correct, just "President"? Do you see "Mr. President" anywhere?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, perhaps there's no need for me to read the whole thing. If you say so, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did Serbs enter Srebrenica? At what time.

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Believe me, information, details, that is something that I was under no obligation to memorise, nor did I want to. Believe me, that I only see these things when I come here now. I recall only a few authentic conversations. I remember how Mladic was arranging with a TV station that it be recorded and then sold. I don't think we have it here. I also remember another conversation of his when he entered himself, but I know longer remember what time it was, at what time of day. And, ultimately, I did not analyse this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why don't we have that intercept, where Mladic was arranging for a TV crew to record something and then to have it sold?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not for this witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I would think that if the witness has any knowledge of that he should be allowed to answer. I don't see why he would be precluded answering [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: then the question should be formulated whether he knew there was such one or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, he just told us that there was. It's just a question of why we don't have it. But I think he might have some information about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You may ask the witness whether such intercept existed, but he take it for granted that such intercept existed. Yes, please go on -- please carry on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies, I wanted to ask the witness this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who decided which intercepts would not be handed over to the Prosecution? That was the gist of my question, although it was put inexpertly. You seem to be positive that you heard that conversation and that it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I am 100 per cent certain that I heard it. That footage was sent -- was sold for 50.000 German marks. I know that for a fact. Now, as for the recording itself, I don't know what its fate was. I don't know what the fate was of other conversations. I don't know how many intercepts were handed over to the Tribunal. I did not use that information. I was simply a person involved in technical matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you heard that there was footage made and sold. But I'm interested in whether you heard Mladic say that he wanted it recorded. Did you record or in another way register that particular conversation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: You will agree that it was a long time ago. I cannot say with any certainty that it exists, but it can certainly be checked whether it does exist or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many intercepts in total did you record over the two years?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: It wasn't two years. If you recall some of the documents, we arrived at that trig point in December 1992, and we used a lot of time to test relay routes, make assessments as to the possibility of intercepting, et cetera. I don't know how many conversations there were. I know that on some days, we barely managed to type it all into the computer, and we needed the assistance of our secretary from headquarters to help us type it all up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it because there were many on a particular day?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because there were many. There were such days when we were physically unable to type it all up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me how many on average, daily?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't follow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how many times did you have me on the line? How many intercepts include me?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Can you tell us what you did with such intercepts which paint me or the Serbian side in a good light?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand. What good light?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you do with such intercepts that could be favourable for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Pardon me. First of all, let me say this: If we heard you - and I will be literal - we even took down jokes you told, let alone other things. Or if we heard anyone else from the leadership, we taped it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us this then: Can you state that everything you recorded, primarily in relation to me, that it is readily available to the parties in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I don't know. I was offered this. I don't know about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you were reviewing the transcripts, did you notice that some were missing? Perhaps some conversations you recall.

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: A lot of time has passed, really. What I said about Mladic a moment ago, I remember it clearly. I simply wanted to use that as an illustration so that you would understand things better. I don't know. I would have to go through the log-book and go down the page to see whether everything's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that log-book exist? Is it available to you so that you could tell us which intercepts were not handed over to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I can't. I can't say which ones were not because I would have to check everything. As far as I remember, parts of that log-book were presented in a trial, so it does exist. Now what was the other thing you asked? Yes, this is what I wanted to say. I remember, for example, some orders, and I never came across those conversations, and I don't know what happened with them. I'm afraid that some transcripts, especially such conversations that were not discussed here, such as the ones over the teleprinters or fax machines, perhaps the transcripts of those were destroyed by the service as unimportant. I don't know. But I believe that these transcripts should all be available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall my oral orders that were intercepted which you did not see here? Because you mentioned orders a moment ago. Whose orders? Mine?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: No, no. I don't recall the reproduced conversations, but I do remember a conversation of yours -- well, I'm not quite certain. But a telefax message was intercepted which followed a round of peace talks in 1995. So a truce was arranged, and the telefax contained an order on the deployment of units. That's what I recall, and I didn't see it here. There are many such conversations of military nature that were perhaps not so interesting to be used here and probably were not made use of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you worked for the Ministry of Interior; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: If you want to discuss that topic, as I may be identified, I'd kindly ask that we move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was your profession at the time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: At the time, I was a teacher of technical skills education.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you able to tell us, in view of the fact that we're in closed session, whether the Ministry of the Interior or, rather, your service, was it a part of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you receive a certificate of your participation in the war? And what are the dates?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I don't know what certificate you mean. I am officially recorded as a participant in the war, and I cannot remember precisely the dates, but I think it's until the 22nd of April, 1996. I think. But I cannot remember when exactly. Let's say it was from September 1991. I cannot remember exactly what it states on that piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: September 1991. All right. And was that as a member of the MUP or a member of the Patriotic League? Which formation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: If you remember - and I'm sure that you do - God forbid that members of the service would be members of the Patriotic League at the time; in 1991, I mean. I worked in the service, and, on that basis, I was granted the time-period as participation in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I wanted to let the parties know that we'll be sitting pursuant to normal schedule today, that given the -- another trial that involves one of the members of the Bench. So if it is convenient, we are minded to take a break now. Yes, it's okay. We are now in open session. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can use that expression without causing confusion, may I introduce Ms. Alicia Kuin, who is a graduate student at the University of Utrecht and who has been working with my team for the last few months. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. Shall we take a break now? For 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, according to your best recollection, are you able to tell us if Mladic asked only for everything to be recorded? Or did he ask for things to be recorded for the purposes of sale? Did he mention the sale, or did you hear later that this was sold later?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Should I repeat what I said? I should. Mladic wanted to cash in on the exclusive footage of the entry of the Army of Republika Srpska to Srebrenica. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you don't remember which station or which crew was in charge of that. Was that some military organisation or a regular TV company?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were several television companies, and maybe even some foreign TV companies. But I really cannot remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember if it was specified what should be recorded, and was everything recorded?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: It was not allowed to film everything. It was just the entry of the Serbian forces to Srebrenica that was recorded, the actual act of the army entering Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we were to look for this transcript, it would be found somewhere, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really tell you if it exists or not. I'm just telling you what I heard. And the people who were working at that location at the time, they heard the same thing. And as far as I can recall, we wrote this down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell us who made the decision and why was this group formed at this location? I don't want to refer to the location.

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I think that, in the course of 1994, we managed to prepare a number of devices that were able to intercept radio-relay lines and monitor telephone conversations. This decision, pursuant to which we were sent to that location, followed an analysis of the monitoring of a certain route, which showed that a large quantity of intelligence was leaking from the citizens who, in conversations among themselves, gave away positions, the number of men, certain actions, and so on and so forth. After that, we were told that we should talk to people from the 2nd Corps of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Army, of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that's how we ended up at this location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you're talking about the leaking of information from conversation of Serb civilians, right, which would be useful to you? Or are you talking about Muslim civilians as well, in this case?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, it was very important to us to acquire intelligence from your side, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you able to tell us, if you remember, if, in late 1994, President Carter secured a four-month truce, which we referred to as Carter's Truce?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I do remember a few such cease-fires for the purposes of negotiation, but I do not remember the individual ones and their time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember that the B&H Army General Staff, on the 5th of January, 1995, issued a directive for combat, which would also affect the enclaves, five days after the signing of that cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, if you heard me correctly, I really don't remember any of that. I wasn't aware of any information that concerned the lines where the actions happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you cannot link the forming of that team and that location with this directive; is that correct? We're talking about late December. And we have a cease-fire that is in effect, and, at the same time, we have that directive being issued. Did you become aware later that you were sent there because of what was contained in the subsequent directive? Why were you sent there in 1994 otherwise?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Late 1994. That was not recorded. End of 1994.

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I tried to explain that we didn't have either the personnel or the material resources, and we did not do that kind of work before. You know that. I mean, it was just a need that we became aware of. Military resources, which was part of the PEB, were not capable of covering the multitude of conversations and the connections that you inherited from the Yugoslav People's Army and started to use yourselves. The estimate -- or the assessment here was that a lot of intelligence that is important could be acquired through the monitoring of those communication routes. And, at the same time, we could take part in this monitoring and augment the insufficient resources. So the fact that we went to this location had nothing to do with any political events, negotiations, any cease-fires or anything like that. There was no connection between these two things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said before the break: "... God forbid that a member of the service would be a member of the Patriotic League." Why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I'm going to try to explain that. You know where I come from. In my town, in 1992 and throughout the war, Bosniak and Serb and Croat colleagues all worked together, and this is different from the area where you were in the leadership so you know that. Perhaps you can mention a Bosniak or not, but I don't think that anyone worked there. So the environment where we worked was still not burdened by such matters. And my position as a member of the service was to be organised apolitically and to cultivate a strictly professional relationship, and this is why I would like to tell you this. Other than the fact that we had active operatives who were Serbs and Croats during the war, shortly before the war, a few colleagues who went to different companies or who were in a different line of work or were retired, offered to join and were taken into the service and spent their entire time there throughout the war. I don't doubt that the SDS or the SDA and the HDZ, had they, at that time, used the options available to them and put their own cadres into the service at the time, but I think that 90 per cent of the people who actually worked there were professionals and it was their job to do what they were doing. I think it's difficult to explain to people who don't come from Bosnia and Herzegovina that in a conflict like that and in a service like that, it's difficult to explain that we had members of all three peoples in the service working at that time. So I'm telling you this in order to reinforce my assertion that it was unthinkable to me at the time to belong to the Patriotic League. To any party, never mind the Patriotic League. And, finally, you also may remember that the MUP was in conflict with the Patriotic League in my town that year, so that all of this indicates the actual situation as it was. I have a problem to explain that to people. People don't understand that. They don't believe it. However, I believe that you do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But I would like the Trial Chamber to know why. Why? What is so irreconcilable between your service and the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I really want to be clear here. I was not part of the operations force that was involved in that kind of thing. I just know about this as phenomena, occurrences. Then there were the conflicts there. After all, you know that the Patriotic League, I mean, these people who were in town, they were moved out of town. They could not stay in town because -- well, let me put it this way. Let me speak as a citizen. Everybody thought that that was unnecessary and that it makes the situation even more complicated because the feeling amongst the citizens themselves was different. No one was in favour of a war. No one believed that there would be a war, and I believe that these multi-ethnic people who worked there where I worked and in the police reflected that kind of feeling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is quite praise-worthy, and I believe you. But I am interested in hearing who was it that Bosnia-Herzegovina was at war with in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, just before the witness answers. I actually really think that the answer at page 33, line 25, to 34, line 3, should be redacted because that would reveal the city that this witness hails from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Line 24 to 3?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry. 25 to 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he mention his -- his town?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The situation he described was unique to that location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll follow your advice.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who was it that Bosnia-Herzegovina was at war with in 1991?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: You're probably asking me that because of that certificate. I wondered myself. Believe me. I was not at war with anyone, but that was the decision made at top-state level, to have this kind of service recognised for those people who were in sub-services and those who were, I think. Let me say: I think. I'm not sure. Those who were in the Patriotic League and -- well, I don't know. I don't know. I really don't know any more than that. I just know that we, members of the MUP, did have those years of service recognised as such. I know that Bosnia and Herzegovina, or, rather, we were not at war with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that some people had war-time service recognised from the 30th of April, 1991, and that that is what the Bosnian law says?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I don't think you're right. This is the first time I hear of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have that, so if we haven't tender it already, we shall do so. All right. Was this service, veterans' service, recognised for Serbs as well, from 1991?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: My colleagues, those people who worked together with me, they had these years of service recognised just as they were in my case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you tap the conversations of members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did you record them; and if you happened to do so, what did you do with these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: A moment ago, I explained that there weren't enough of us to follow you. Really. There were very few people there, and there was very little equipment too. When reviewing the frequency, if we came across the route that was used by our side, if I can put it that way, because -- you know what, to tell you the truth, I don't know even know whether the army used RU-800. I mean whether we had these channels at all, I really have no idea. But if we were to come across these civilian routes we would not really dwell on that. We didn't have time for that. There was no need for us to deal with that because we had plenty of work on the other side. Even more than we could handle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any problems due to the existence of --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can we move into private session just for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The other infrastructure that existed there of the United Nations, did that hinder you in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean, if I am going to refer to this infrastructure, I would like us to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So is it correct that one technician would be recording what was heard and the other one would be transcribing what was heard on that tape?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Everyone did everything at that particular location. You will see that in one particular case one employee did the recording and in another case that same person transcribed something. So what does this look like in practice? Two men are sitting there and they have equipment in front of them. At this point in time there is nothing to be reproduced. They are following this, and then the very next moment, both of them are recording. After that, they would agree that one of them would go over and transcribe what was heard and the other one continues to listen to what was being said. So that is, in real terms, what the situation is like in that room. Or if there's nothing happening at a particular moment, both of them would do that, and they would listen as well, and then they would pause in their reproduction or transcription if they would have to turn on the recording devices in the meantime, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So could you tell us then: Was it not possible, if not even customary, that the person who was doing the transcribing did not necessarily listen and record as well?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we do agree that those comments and explanations and so on and so forth were created by the person who was doing the transcribing, not the person who was doing the recording.

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: In the specific case that we dealt with previously, when we dealt with Gvero, the comment followed after listening to all the conversations on that day, and then the employee wrote that, on that day, at that location, there was only Gvero. When an employee hears a conversation, then he writes down the time, the route, and the participants. So the person who is going to transcribe that can use that for making the heading, where it says exactly what the time and frequency, channel and participants were. So what does that mean in practical terms. The person who takes the tape in order to transcribe what was heard, he will take this sheet of paper where all of this is written down and he will see that those introductions were heard, the ones that we talked about a minute ago, and that is not on the tape so that is what he uses for writing up the first sentence. So that is where this co-operation is indispensable between the person who is doing the recording and the person who is doing the transcription.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at 65 ter 23644 without it being broadcast. It may have been made a P exhibit already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Without referring to the location, can you tell us whether the marked location is where you worked and whether the map depicts the area you were able to monitor?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes. This is the location where we worked, but it is not the whole area we could monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you could cover a wider area. But what is on the map was covered by you, was it not?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, let's put it that way. I would have to analyse everything, but I do know that from the location, we covered this entire area and beyond.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The part we see here, could you monitor it without any problems? Under excellent conditions, so to say.

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree. Nothing is in excellent conditions or open to monitoring in Bosnia because of the terrain. It was always possible that some communication could not be monitored, in valleys, at the foot of mountains, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did it happen that you could hear one participant and not the other?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I'll try to explain. I hope you will be able to understand. One participant has the ability of two-way communication. That is to say, something I say and something the other person is saying. It could happen that we heard well the person calling, whereas the person on the other end was not heard because we could not locate the so-called duplex frequency. By hard work, we managed, sometimes, and on another piece of equipment, we would find the other frequency. And in that case, we would have both ends and we could record a full conversation. There was another thing. Depending on the quality of the micro-telephonic combination, that is to say, the headset, and the signal quality, we frequently, by combining the two, we could hear the other person as well, but it was always the weaker signal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you could listen in even in cases when a VRS communication was protected, but you could break through our protective measures?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, when I was up there, I didn't even know what protected communication you had. Let me mention an example. For example, we could hear a participant say, Is this communication protected? And then the other one would say, Yes, talk freely. But we could hear it all. Whatever traffic was protected, it was usually by teleprinter encryption as well as telefax signals, but not for us because by that time we had equipment which could decode. Another piece of information. I think in 1995, perhaps in July or August, encrypted telephone lines were used by your side and then we could only pick up the scrambled signal. We knew it was speech protected by a certain encryption method.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see the bottom right-hand side of the map? The two front lines depicted there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you listen to that area too?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I don't know how technically versed you are in telephonic communication, but let me try and explain. Say a person is in a cave which is completely protected and that person makes a phone call to his friend in Bijeljina, he needs to become part of the system which transmits signal through air, and that is where such communication is open to interception. What am I trying to say? One could call from this area and use part of the route that was intercepted. However, if that person had a conversation within the area you marked, then perhaps we would be unable to hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you're discussing wire connections or radio-relay connections?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, it is wire connection from here to the next switchboard. But as from that point on, it uses the parabolic antenna and travels through the air, becoming open to interception. I believe many VRS officers were confused by this, thinking that they communicated by wire, wire communication, whereas it was not protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you at your post in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: What post?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The feature where you worked. Were you at your work post?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you follow communication between you and the locations that are marked here?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Are you asking me if we had communication with the area that is marked here? Did we have direct communication? Is that what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you probably did not, but they probably communicated with their corps. Did you record that? And were you able to follow what was going on?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: My group did not have such communication with the area. I don't know of anyone from the corps being in communication with that location, since I know the location itself was used only for interception.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have means of electronic insight into what was going on in the area; and, if so, how?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: When Srebrenica fell, we did not have a possibility to monitor. We did monitor what you communicated, but during a period we were able to pick up hand-held radio signals used by these enormous groups of people leaving the enclave. We listened to that, and we listened to your hand-held radios, too, when it became accessible. I can no longer say which were the locations that we could monitor at that point in time, but we were 100 per cent certain that there were hand-held radios used by those people or your side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say "your side," or "my side," do you mean Serbian hand-held radios?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: No. I didn't have in mind your personal hand-held radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you record the conversations between these enormous groups of people breaking through?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How come? Why did you not?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: This is why. From the conversations we could hear, we realised that those enormous groups containing thousands of people were going somewhere. They were on the move. On the other side, we could hear Serb forces using radio communication to confuse them and misinform them, which was the kind of warfare that was used at the time. We were trying to listen to the Serb hand-held radios and disturb their signal, but I don't think we succeeded. They were too far away. In any case, we monitored the situation, and, at some point, I know that everyone in Zvornik was being mobilised, including the police, and it was stated that an enormous group of 3.000 people was moving towards Zvornik to attack them. But they didn't know that those people were actually lost. They didn't know where they were, and your side seemed to believe that there was an attack. They were simply trying to flee and were disoriented. Our goal was to scramble or block your signal. That was what we were trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that when it comes to electronic communication, the sides used different tactics, such as jamming, misinforming, sending messages that were aimed at confusing the other side?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: That's a separate story. I was discussing a very specific event. Members of the VRS were trying to have those people, those masses, as we learned later on, to lead them to ambushes. That was the purpose. Of course, special warfare is a different thing, such as misinformation, et cetera, but I don't think that is the topic we are supposed to cover here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell when there were two Serb officers talking whether they were misinforming intentionally as to the numbers or intentions? Could you tell they were doing that in order to tell your superiors that such information should not be taken for granted?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: The information we obtained by monitoring our radio-relay routes, I can state that no misinformation occurred on that communication because we heard frequently the participants saying, This is protected, they can't pick this up, et cetera. So there was no misinformation there. When it comes to the flight of the people from the enclave to free territory, they were being misinformed by way of hand-held radios, and the other side was saying, Move this way, move that way. That's where our people are, et cetera. That is how it took place. Perhaps you have some other information. But based on the conversations we heard, we never concluded that there was intentional misinformation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's leave July 1995 aside. But, in principle, were you ever in a situation of doubting certain information and believing that they were put out there in order to emphasise them or de-emphasise them, in order to deceive the enemy, simply speaking?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, I would restrict myself to what I was given, and I would limit myself to the route that we were monitoring. And the other possibilities, I would not really speak about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who decided --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, could I tender the map, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it is part of his associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That is what I assumed, but I didn't get confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who decided about the priorities, what should be listened to and what should be a work priority?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, we had determined the priorities. The priority was this route. Everything that went through that route, especially calls by top leadership on the Serbian side. Sometimes when there was no activity there, the operator could make his own decisions on other channels, how important a conversation was, and act on his own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how did you decide? How did the Serbs deceive those who were engaged in the breakthrough? Did they pretend to be Muslim stations? How did you discover that they were misinforming them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: We would listen for a long time. I think that at one point somebody from the 2nd Corps PEB, since they did have more powerful jamming devices, suggested to us that that was the -- how it was, and so we focussed more there. We focussed more on certain locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If they had wanted to do that, that would mean that they were on the same frequency as the Muslims -- Muslim hand-held stations. Otherwise, they wouldn't be able to hear them; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Of course. They did find them. They could hear them. They would set themselves on their frequencies and then begin to plant misinformation. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then in jamming Serbian hand-held stations, you were also jamming the Muslim ones? Or were you able to filter that? I mean, if you were on the same frequency, you were jamming both sides; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, I hear you speaking, but, as soon as I begin to speak, somebody is going to push the button and start jamming my conversation. So, in the same way, we would listen to people from the enclave and then when they would start to broadcast from the other side, we would press the button in order to jam the communication. And now, since we're talking about this, I can say this. One operative who was at this location, his close relative came from the area. He broke through, and when he spoke with him about this, about the jamming, the monitoring, and all of these things, this person from the enclave told him that in one place, he saw about 3.000 dead people just in front of a wood, and he managed to survive. And he confirmed this information to us. I haven't talked about this here. Nobody asked me anything about that, but I'm telling that there were people who took part in the events. I don't know where this location is. I didn't go there, but this person's close relative confirmed that they were listening as these large groups of people were being directed or guided to come to these locations where the executions took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about them being guided to ambushes. Are you saying that these people were led to minefields and -- I mean, what were these people being led to? And how do you know that this was a Serb doing it and not a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, I would rather not talk about this. I would ask you that. What I'm saying is that in that period we heard the other side, the Serbian side, use the communications to misinform the people who were in these woods. What I was talking about now -- I mean, I don't know if they were guided to minefields or something else. All I'm saying is that in a conversation after the events, a conversation with somebody's cousin, information was confirmed that people were led to ambushes and that many of these people were killed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this is exactly what I am asking you. Were you able to see by electronic means what was going on in those woods? Were you able to see what the number of dead was and how they were killed, how they died? Was it by artillery fire, in minefields, was it infantry weapons? And did you know about the number of casualties and the localities?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: We couldn't know anything about the number of casualties, about the places. And precisely because we didn't know, I think that we were not successful in the jamming. I think that they were too far. We didn't know what the numbers were, what the routes they were moving along were. We didn't know anything. We knew that the killings were going on. You could hear it from the conversations. And in Zvornik, when they would pick up and say, Well, 3.000 of them are coming towards us, we knew those kinds of things, that sort of information from the conversations. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you record this important communication?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, I already said that we didn't record these things, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's still not clear to me how -- well, let's clarify one thing. If a Serb hand-held radio was used to misinform the Muslim side, would that person introduce themselves as a Muslim or as a Serb?

utterances.speaker: KDZ357: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Of course, the person would introduce themselves as a Muslim. Otherwise how would they be able to plant the misinformation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
